rows.text: ## Why this one first The inbox was the only place where volume and a measurable outcome met. Every other candidate needed a survey to tell whether it had worked. You cannot gate a release on a metric you have to ask about. ## What made it shippable Three things, in this order. An eval set built from tickets that already had answers, so there was a known-good answer to compare against. Tracing on every call, so a bad answer could be traced to the retrieval step rather than argued about. A cost ceiling per ticket, checked in the same CI job as the evals. ## What I built, in order | Part | What it's for | | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Eval set from real tickets | A known-good answer to check every change against, before it reaches a customer. | | [Model Context Protocol](/glossary/mcp) as the tool boundary | Keeps what the agent may call explicit and narrow, instead of improvised inside a prompt. | | [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io) tracing | Every call recorded, so a wrong answer traces back to a retrieval step, not a guess. | | GitHub Actions eval gate | Runs the eval set on every change so a regression blocks the merge before it reaches a ticket. | ## What I would do differently I built the first eval set from tickets that already had good answers. Seasonality made the first week of results look better than the system was. Sampling across a longer window would have caught that before anyone celebrated.

rows.text: The distinction that matters is between a single prompt and response and a task an agent sees through to the end. A chatbot that answers one question is not agentic. A system that reads a support ticket, looks up the order, drafts a refund and issues it is agentic. Nobody scripted that exact sequence in advance. Engineering teams build this pattern because it automates the cross-system judgement calls that used to need a person. Security reviewers and boards ask about it separately from the model itself, because the risk changes once a system can act, not only speak. A wrong sentence in a chat reply is embarrassing. A wrong action against a live order or a payment has already happened by the time anyone notices, because nothing stood between the decision and the outcome.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It comes up the moment a pitch or a product description says "agent" instead of "assistant". A security reviewer's next question is almost always what the agent can do without asking first. The reviewer asks because that is where the real exposure sits, not the model choice. A board hears "agentic" and correctly hears "this thing takes actions on its own." That is a different risk conversation than a chatbot that only produces text. ## What to do about it List every action an agent can take, not just what it can say, and sign off on each as a separate risk. Set a real limit on what it can do without a person confirming first, especially anything that spends money, touches a customer record, or sends something external. Log every tool call, so a bad outcome traces to a specific decision. Evals belong here: test the whole action chain, not just the model's replies.

rows.text: AI governance sits above the technology itself. It covers who owns each AI system, what data it may touch, which use cases are off limits, and who signs off before a system reaches customers. That shows up as a register of the systems in use, a policy engineers actually follow, and a review step before anything new goes live. A customer's procurement team asks for it during a security review. A board asks after a pilot nears production, once someone raises who is liable for a bad call. Regulators ask for pieces of it too, through frameworks like the NIST AI RMF and standards like ISO/IEC 42001. In practice, it changes three things. Someone specific owns each AI system, instead of it belonging to whichever team built it. A new system needs sign-off before it touches customer data. A written answer exists the day a customer or auditor asks for one.

rows.text: The EU AI Act calls this a fundamental rights impact assessment. Article 27 requires it from deployers that are public-law bodies or private entities delivering a public service. It also applies to any deployer using a high-risk system to score creditworthiness. The same goes for pricing life and health insurance. The assessment has to name the process the system sits inside, how often it runs, and which people or groups it is likely to affect. It has to describe the human oversight in place, and the governance and complaint routes that take effect if a risk appears. The deployer sends the finished assessment to the national market surveillance authority. Article 27 lets this assessment build on an existing data protection impact assessment rather than repeat it. Where the two overlap, the newer document only has to add what the DPIA does not already answer.

rows.text: For almost every high-risk system, the provider checks its own work against the rules and signs a declaration, with no outside reviewer involved. Only biometric-identification systems sometimes need an independent outside checker, a "notified body," to sign off instead. Article 43 sets this split by Annex III area, the EU AI Act's list of high-risk use cases. Every area except biometric identification uses Annex VI, the self-check route with no notified body involved. Biometric identification uses Annex VII's notified-body route wherever harmonised standards are not fully applied or do not yet exist. Harmonised standards are the detailed technical rules the Commission recognises as proof of compliance. The assessment is not a one-time formality. Any substantial change to a system after launch triggers a new one, under whichever route applied the first time. The one exception is a system that keeps learning after deployment. A provider can plan for that drift in advance and record it in the technical documentation before the first assessment. Later changes that stay within that plan do not reopen the process.

rows.text: GDPR Article 35 makes this review mandatory, not a judgement call, in three situations. One is large-scale profiling with legal or similarly significant effects. Another is large-scale processing of special-category data, such as health or biometric records. The third is systematic large-scale monitoring of a public space. Most consequential AI systems land in the first of these by default. The assessment has to describe the processing and why it is necessary. It has to assess the risk to the people concerned and set out the measures that reduce it. Where the company has appointed a data protection officer, the company must consult that officer while it carries out the assessment. Signing off afterward does not count. Where the system is high-risk under the EU AI Act, Article 26 also refers to the DPIA. A deployer must draw on the information the provider supplies under Article 13 when carrying out this GDPR assessment. The two obligations end up sharing evidence, not separate files.

rows.text: Formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. It sorts AI systems into a risk ladder, from banned practices, to a high-risk category, to a lighter set of transparency duties. High-risk covers things like hiring, credit and law enforcement. The lighter duties apply to systems such as chatbots. The Act leaves everything else largely unregulated. Obligations scale with the tier. High-risk systems carry duties such as a conformity assessment, technical documentation, human oversight, and registration in an EU database. The Act applies to any company whose AI system is used in the EU, not only companies based there. That is why a US-based startup with European customers cannot treat this as someone else's problem. In practice, the Act changes what "we did not think about that" costs. For a high-risk use case, a company now needs a documented risk assessment and a named point of human oversight. The company also needs evidence of both, ready before a regulator or a customer's legal team asks.

rows.text: A system reaches the category one of two ways. Article 6(1) covers the first: a safety component of a product already regulated under EU product-safety law, or that product itself. Medical devices and machinery are examples. That product-safety law already requires third-party conformity assessment. Annex III covers the second: eight listed use-case areas, among them biometric identification, employment decisions, credit scoring and law enforcement. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk just by falling into one of those areas, with no product-safety law involved at all. A system inside Annex III can still escape the label under Article 6(3), for four narrow reasons. One is a limited procedural task, such as reformatting an application into a standard template. Another is improving a human decision already made, such as tidying a report's wording without changing its recommendation. A third is detecting a deviation without replacing human judgement, such as flagging an unusual transaction for a fraud analyst to review. The fourth is a preparatory task ahead of someone else's assessment, such as gathering a loan applicant's documents before a human underwriter looks at them. None of the four applies to profiling: a system that profiles individual people is high-risk regardless.

It specifies requirements for an AI management system: the recurring policies, roles and processes that govern how an organisation develops, provides or uses AI. It uses the same Plan-Do-Check-Act structure as other ISO management-system standards, such as ISO/IEC 27001 for information security. They ask because certification gives them a documented, externally checked answer instead of a vendor's own claim. Working towards the standard means three things: writing down a risk-assessment method, running an inventory of AI systems, and reviewing that inventory on a schedule. Engineering teams adopt one to stop rebuilding the same authentication and logging code in every project that touches a model. rows.text: ## Why it comes up A security questionnaire almost always asks how the company controls and logs access to the model provider. "Each team manages its own API key" is a poor answer. A board or customer asks a version of the same question after a well-publicised leak elsewhere. In that leak, a prompt carrying sensitive data reached a third-party model unlogged. Without a gateway, nobody can produce every prompt sent to a vendor last month. ## What to do about it Put one gateway in front of every model call before adding a second application that talks to a model, not after. Route all API keys through it rather than into individual codebases, and log every request and response. Redact anything that looks like a customer identifier or a secret before it leaves. Solid open-source and hosted options already exist, so this is rarely worth building in house. ## The gateway as a governance control A written policy says what staff may do with a model. A gateway is the control that enforces it, because every model call passes through one place where the policy runs. It decides who may call which model, strips sensitive data before it leaves, applies rate limits, and logs each request and response. That log is the evidence a security questionnaire asks for: it shows the policy ran, not only that it exists. The limit is coverage: a gateway controls only the calls that go through it, so an application that calls a vendor directly sits outside the control. The [LLM Gateway Governance Config](/resources/llm-gateway-governance-config) gives a policy file format for one.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up In this site's reading, it comes up when a team connects an [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow) to its own systems and a security reviewer asks what the agent can touch. "Open protocol" can sound like a safety claim. It is not one. A 2026 sheet from the US National Security Agency (NSA) says MCP's security posture "remains uneven and highly dependent on implementation discipline rather than protocol guarantees". The sheet cites the November 2025 revision of the specification. ## What to do about it The model picks which tool to call, and text it reads can steer that choice. That is [prompt injection](/glossary/prompt-injection). The MCP project's security policy says a report that an LLM invoked an unexpected tool is not an MCP vulnerability. So the limits go in the host and the servers, as [guardrails](/glossary/guardrails) in code. Give each server only the access its task needs. That is least privilege. The NSA sheet recommends that tool execution be constrained and sandboxed. ## Where the specification stops The specification, in its 28 July 2026 revision, names who should do the first three jobs. The protocol does not check that anyone does. - Approval before a tool runs: the host. There should always be a [human in the loop](/glossary/human-in-the-loop) who can deny a call. - Checks on inputs and access: each server. Servers must validate all tool inputs and implement proper access controls. - Logs: the host's clients. They should log tool usage, which feeds [observability](/glossary/observability). - Local servers: a local server the client starts runs with the client's privileges. The policy says the SDK's STDIO transport, which does the starting, "is not a sandbox".

rows.text: The format comes from a 2018 paper. The paper proposed model cards as a response to models shipping with no consistent account of how their makers had actually tested them. A rigorous card reports evaluation broken out by group: race, geographic location, sex, skin type. NIST's risk management framework expects the same thing in substance. A model should be explained, validated and documented, not simply shipped. A vendor who has actually done that evaluation work typically wants to show the results, since they usually help on some axis. One who cannot produce a card has most likely skipped the evaluation itself, not just the paperwork describing it.

rows.text: Direct injection comes from whoever is typing into the box, phrased to override the model's own hidden starting instructions, its system prompt. Indirect injection is the more dangerous form. It arrives inside content the model retrieves on its own: a webpage it is summarising, a resume it is screening. No attacker ever touches the model directly. Multimodal systems add a further variant, since an instruction can hide inside an image processed alongside ordinary text. It has kept that position through every edition of the list, most recently the 2026 revision. The reason is structural: the model reads instructions and untrusted data through the same channel. A filter tuned on known patterns still misses a novel phrasing. Every mitigation available today reduces the odds of a successful attack; none removes them.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It is the first thing a security reviewer probes on any AI feature that reads outside content. rows.text: Article 3 defines a provider by two acts done together. The first is developing the system, or having someone else develop it. The second is placing it on the market or putting it into service, under the provider's own name or trademark. Payment is irrelevant. Giving the system away under your own brand still makes you the provider. A deployer is defined by use, not branding: using the system under the deployer's own authority. The only carve-out is personal, non-professional activity. A company using a tool internally is a deployer even if it never touches a customer. That test has a sharp edge. A company that fine-tunes a vendor's model and ships the result under its own product name has made itself the provider of that product. It does not matter that it built none of the underlying model. Owning the brand is what matters, not how much of the system the company actually wrote.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It surfaces in a contract negotiation once both sides realise the label matters more than expected. A provider owes technical documentation and a conformity assessment, while a deployer mainly owes human oversight and monitoring. A board hears about it when a vendor's contract quietly assigns the company duties it assumed the vendor carried. Getting the role wrong can leave a company holding an obligation nobody budgeted for. ## What to do about it Run the provider-or-deployer test per system, not per company. Rebranding one vendor's model can make a company a provider for that product while it stays a deployer for everything else it merely uses. Write the answer into the AI register alongside the risk tier, since a security questionnaire will eventually ask for both. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) is where I answer this kind of question inside a live negotiation. ## Deployer obligations checklist Article 26 of the EU AI Act sets these duties for a deployer of a [high-risk AI system](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system). They apply to high-risk systems only. The provider carries a separate set of duties, and public authorities and some biometric uses carry further duties in the same Article. - Use the system as the provider's instructions for use say. - Assign [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) to people who have the competence, training, authority and support to do it. - Make sure the input data you control is relevant and representative for the system's purpose. - Monitor the system against those instructions. If you have reason to think it presents a risk, tell the provider, importer or distributor and the market surveillance authority without undue delay, and suspend its use. - Report a [serious incident](/glossary/serious-incident-reporting) at once, to the provider first. - Keep the logs the system generates, as far as you control them, for at least six months unless other law says otherwise. - If you are an employer, tell the workers' representatives and the affected workers before you use a high-risk system at work. - Tell people when a high-risk system listed in Annex III makes or helps make a decision about them. - Use the provider's information for your [data protection impact assessment](/glossary/dpia) where one is required. - Cooperate with the competent authorities.

rows.text: Red teaming means deliberately trying to break an AI system, the way a motivated attacker or a determined bad-faith user would, before they actually do. It aims at finding the failure nobody wrote a test case for, not at confirming cases already known to work.

rows.text: A red team engagement produces a different kind of output than a test run. It is a list of the specific techniques that worked, detailed enough for someone else to reproduce the failure. It also carries a judgement on what an attacker could actually do with it. That reproducibility is what separates a report from an anecdote about something that broke once. NIST's generative AI profile recommends red teaming as a check against specific categories of harm, including information leakage and harmful content generation. Those failures depend on someone actively trying to cause them; they rarely show up in ordinary use. The finding that matters is the one nobody predicted going in.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up Boards and security reviewers increasingly ask for it by name, rather than accepting "we ran evals" as a full answer. An eval suite built by the same team that built the system tends to test what that team already expected to go wrong. It matters more, not less, once a system can take actions or read outside content. A missed failure then moves from a bad reply to a completed action. ## What to do about it Budget real time, not an afternoon, for someone to actively try prompt injection, data extraction and off-limits requests. Do it against the actual live system, not a sanitised demo. Write down exactly what broke, and fix the underlying guardrail, not just the one example that happened to get tried. I treat this as part of shipping in the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint), folding findings back into the eval suite before launch.

rows.text: The document store is usually a vector index. The system converts passages into embeddings, numerical representations of meaning, and matches a query against them by similarity, not exact keyword. Matching on meaning lets the system find a relevant passage even when the question shares none of the same words as the document. OWASP, the group that publishes widely used security-risk lists, tracks this as its own risk category. In a shared vector database, one customer's data can leak into another customer's results. Embeddings carry a second risk: someone can sometimes invert them to recover the source text they came from. Both risks sit inside the retrieval layer, invisible to anyone reviewing only the model or the prompts it receives.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up Procurement asks "is this RAG, or did you train on our data," because the two have different data-handling implications. RAG typically sends only retrieved snippets to the model at query time, rather than baking a customer's content into the model's own weights. It also comes up once someone questions accuracy. A wrong answer usually traces to a retrieval problem, not a flaw in the model itself. ## What to do about it Control access at the document-store level, not only at the chat interface. RAG will surface anything in the index to anyone who can ask the right question, regardless of who is meant to see it. Treat the document store itself as a data-classification boundary. Check what happens when a document containing hidden instructions ends up inside it. That exact scenario is one of the checks in the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint).

rows.text: The duty applies once a malfunction leads to death, serious harm, or a serious breach of someone's fundamental rights. Article 73 sets the default deadline at fifteen days from when the provider becomes aware of the incident. The duty also covers serious harm to property or the environment, not only harm to people, though that case still runs on the fifteen-day default.

rows.text: GDPR Article 28 calls the AI vendor the processor and your company the controller. It gives the processor two ways to add a sub-processor. Specific authorisation names the sub-processor up front, so the controller signs off by name. General authorisation lets the processor add sub-processors as needed, but it has to tell the controller first and give a real chance to object. Either way, the processor must pass down the same data-protection obligations it owes directly, in the contract itself, not just a notice. The chain does not stop at one level either. The processor often runs its own infrastructure through a further sub-processor, such as a cloud host or a fine-tuning partner. That passes the same flow-down obligation another level down. Asking for the sub-processor list is really asking how many hops sit between a company's data and the last party that can actually see it.

Figures are from the abstract. | | DORA report, September 2025 | Reported by people | Survey of nearly 5,000 people. More than 80% say AI raised their productivity. | A snapshot. DORA describes comparisons, not effects. Published by a vendor (Google Cloud). | Reported figures disagree. Executives report little impact, while technical workers report large gains. They were asked different questions. Technical workers were asked about their own speed and the value of their work. Executives were asked about employment and productivity over three years. The first three rows disagree in size and sign, and METR flags both of its own results as limited. In February 2026 METR said it believes developers are likely more sped up in early 2026. It called its own data "only very weak evidence" of the size of the gain. Any sentence that says AI makes people faster or slower ages quickly. A survey of your own staff belongs in the reported group. METR says survey estimates tend to be larger than field-experiment estimates. ## What do the usual adoption panels count? The panels below are the usual ones in the sources cited here. That is an inference, not a count. Each tool defines an active user its own way. Figures from two tools do not compare. | Source | What counts as active | | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | GitHub Copilot usage metrics | At least two active days in the trailing 28 to be placed in a usage phase. GitHub says "Passive" is not a measure of inactivity. | | Microsoft 365 Copilot Dashboard | Usage levels over a rolling 12 weeks. A returning user has at least one action in both the current and the previous period. | | DORA 2025 report | No log rule. Adoption is a survey factor made of reliance, trust and reflexive use. | Each panel below has a reason it misleads. | Measure | What it counts | Why it misleads | | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Seats or licences | Money spent. | In GitHub's reports, seat data is not included. It sits in a separate user-management API. | | Daily or weekly active users | One event in a window. | The window and the event differ by vendor, as the table above shows. | | Usage frequency, prompt counts | How often. | DORA's 2024 report, also published by Google Cloud, said measuring usage frequency is "likely not as meaningful as measuring reliance". | | Lines of code accepted, pull requests merged | Output volume. | GitHub calls its lines figure directional. A preprint on Cursor, covering open-source projects, found a short jump in lines added and lasting rises in static-analysis warnings and complexity. Faros, a vendor, found that teams with high adoption completed 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, with 91% longer review time and no significant link to company-level improvement. Its data is observational. | | Acceptance rate | Suggestions taken. | In a 2022 preprint on Copilot users, it tracked how productive users said they felt, rather than how long the accepted code lasted. | | Vendor hours saved and ROI | Action counts times fixed minutes times a wage. | Microsoft builds assisted hours from action counts, fixed minutes per action, and meeting recaps counted by meeting length. A default hourly rate then values them. GitHub says its ROI figures are estimates rather than exact financial results. | | Self-reported speed-up | Opinion. | METR says that in its 2025 trial people overestimated the effect on their task time by 40 percentage points. METR now marks that result out of date. | | Vendor resolution or deflection | Conversations that ended. | Intercom counts a customer who leaves without asking again as resolved, and charges for it, even if the customer is unhappy, unless its agent escalates. | | Adoption multiplier | Engaged users against passive users. | GitHub divides the average merged pull requests of engaged users by that of passive users. That compares people who chose the tool with people who did not, so it cannot isolate the tool's effect. That is an inference, not a GitHub statement. | DORA's 2025 report says: "The conversation must shift from adoption to effective use." DORA's page on measurement frameworks calls it a "common misconception that logs-based metrics are objective". None of the sources cited here shows a usage count predicting a business result. The research behind this article found no independent study that tests whether a usage-based adoption metric predicts outcomes. ## What should adoption telemetry measure instead? This set is a synthesis of the evidence above. No source states it in these words. Sort every number by where it came from. Logs show what people did. Surveys show what people said. The system where the work is recorded shows what happened there, and a randomised trial compares like against like. No one of these is the whole truth on its own. Six measures hold up better, and each has a limit. | Measure | Question it answers | What it cannot tell you | | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | | Coverage | How much AI use at work runs through approved tools? | Whether those tools help. | | Paid versus active, and retention by team | Which seats sit unused, and do people who tried a tool keep using it? | Whether the tool works. | | One outcome per use case | Did the outcome agreed before rollout move, against a baseline or a comparison group? | Why it moved, if there is no comparison. | | Delivery health (engineering use cases) | Did throughput or instability get worse as use grew? | Whether the use case pays off. | | Cost per outcome | What does one unit of the outcome cost? | Whether it is the right outcome. | | A short repeated survey | Do people trust the output, rely on it, and say where it gets in the way? | Whether work got faster. Read it as opinion. | The first two rows are diagnostics. Coverage is a governance question about where AI is used. Paid versus active use and retention show where a tool sits unused, which wastes money and points to a training or workflow problem. In this set, only the third row can show value. Put the weight on the outcome, delivery health, cost and survey rows, and read the survey as opinion. Delivery health is on the list because DORA's 2025 report, published by Google Cloud, found AI adoption going with higher delivery throughput and still with higher instability. DORA describes that as a comparison in a snapshot, not an effect. This agrees with the [approach page](/approach). The measures here add one line. Telemetry shows whether use lasted. An outcome measure shows whether it worked. These are different jobs. The [evals in CI article](/blog/evals-in-ci-for-llm-agents) covers testing a change before it ships. Adoption telemetry asks whether people keep using the system. ## How do you tell whether it worked? Agree the outcome before rollout. Read it from the system that already records it, such as ticketing, CI or your CRM, and not from the AI tool's own logs. The [pilot article](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) covers how to pick an outcome you can measure. The support-agent study in the table read its outcome, issues resolved per hour, from work-system data and not from tool logs. It used a staggered rollout. Then compare against something. A clean comparison is hard, even for researchers. METR's 2026 follow-up produced what it called an unreliable signal. METR's stated reasons include developers choosing not to participate rather than work without AI. It also lists developers becoming more selective about which tasks they submitted. A company of 30 to 300 people will probably not do better than a before-and-after view. That is an inference, not a finding. ## What should you check before collecting data about people? The rules below are general rules for monitoring staff, applied here by analogy. The sources cited here include no regulator text or court decision on AI usage logs. Start with the risk that is easy to miss. A team count built to plan training can turn into a person-level view used to judge performance. The ICO, the UK regulator, gives a clear example. Data collected to manage workspace capacity should not be re-used for performance management without a new lawful basis and a test of necessity and proportionality. That is UK law, not EU law. Treat a log that names a person as personal data about staff. The GDPR asks for a stated purpose, no more data than needed and no longer retention than needed (Article 5). Screen the plan for a [DPIA](/glossary/dpia) first. The Article 29 Working Party's 2017 guidelines list systematic monitoring and data about vulnerable people among their criteria. Employees may count as vulnerable because of the power imbalance. Meeting two criteria means a DPIA in most cases. Whether a usage dashboard counts as systematic monitoring depends on how person-level it is. That is an inference, not a regulator's ruling. Do not rely on staff consent. The same body said consent is highly unlikely to be a legal basis for data processing at work, unless employees can refuse without adverse consequence. That opinion was written under the old Data Protection Directive, so treat it as persuasive guidance, not current law. The Federal Labour Court (1 ABR 20/21, 8 March 2022) reads this as objective suitability: a device counts if it can collect such data, whatever the employer intends. That case concerned Microsoft Office 365, where the parties did not dispute that the data could be used to check behaviour or performance. Applying it to AI usage logs is an inference. | Statute and court decision, both read in the original. | | Netherlands | Works Councils Act, article 27(1): the works council must consent to rules on the processing and protection of staff personal data. It must also consent to provisions aimed at or suitable for checking presence, behaviour or performance, where they cover all or a group of staff. | Secondary copy of the statute. The official text was not read. | | France | CNIL: a monitoring device must pass tests of justification and proportionality, go to staff representatives (the CSE, at employers with 50 or more staff) and be announced to staff beforehand. | Regulator guidance, dated 9 July 2026, read in the original French and paraphrased here. | Keep three things off any dashboard: rankings of named people, prompt content and re-use for performance reviews. The reasons are the ICO example above, the GDPR rule on data minimisation and a warning from DX, a vendor of measurement software. DX warns against using these metrics to judge individuals and says code volume is "particularly susceptible to gaming". Claude Code's documentation says prompt text is off by default. It includes the signed-in user's email, and the documentation tells operators to filter it at their own backend if that is a concern. That is an inference, not something the documentation says: the choice between named and team data sits at your own collector. Set a smallest group you will show, so that a count cannot point at one person. Microsoft's Viva Insights asks administrators to set a minimum group size of at least five. That is a product setting, not a legal figure, and the sources cited here give no legal threshold. The same page says the end-user opt-out does not apply to Copilot usage data, which stays available at the row level. That suggests a group-size floor limits what a report shows, not what is stored. That is an inference. Tell staff before the first log is collected. The CNIL says staff must be told beforehand. The ICO says to seek and document workers' views unless there is a good reason not to. The [acceptable use policy article](/blog/ai-acceptable-use-policy-for-a-50-person-company) covers the policy itself, not the telemetry behind it. ## Where does the dashboard template fit? The [Adoption Telemetry Dashboard Template](/resources/adoption-telemetry-dashboard-template) turns these measures into eight panels. Paid versus active and retention become two panels, and the survey splits into trust and policy clarity. Each panel names the question it answers, the data source and the decision it supports. It is a page to copy into your own tool, not a live dashboard. The coverage panel reads gateway logs, sign-in app lists, expense lines, API bills and the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register). The [register article](/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-system-register-in-a-week) shows how to build one. The [unapproved tools answer](/faq/what-do-we-do-about-tools-staff-are-already-using-without-approval) covers what to do about tools staff already use without approval. The [gateway config](/resources/llm-gateway-governance-config) already sets rate limits per team, not per user. The [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) builds a dashboard that shows tracing and cost per outcome side by side. Its page promises no other panels. The [fractional CAIO retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) includes a review of every AI initiative, shadow tools included. ## What does this article leave out? It reports no client results. The method comes from public studies and vendor documents. Most of the experimental evidence predates agentic tools, so treat each figure as a dated finding. It does not say which baseline method suits your company, which person-level views to allow or who should run the privacy screening. Those depend on your company, your country and your staff representatives. It does not say whether a plain count dashboard is an AI system under the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act), and no source cited here settles that. It is a summary of public texts, not legal advice. Take the legal questions to your data protection officer or counsel.

rows.text: An AI acceptable use policy only earns its place once it decides who approves a new AI tool and which data tier may reach which category of vendor. Beyond that, it decides whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer or a contract. It also decides when the company must tell a customer they are dealing with an AI system. Most templates answer the first two questions and stay quiet on the rest. That is exactly why staff read them once and then ignore them. A policy this size needs one named owner, not a committee. It also needs a review interval short enough to catch the tool people started using without asking. ISO/IEC 42001 treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, not a standalone document. The EU AI Act already requires disclosure once an AI system talks to a customer directly. Skip the enforcement clause and none of the rest holds.

rows.text: Most companies between 30 and 300 people already have staff using AI tools, whether or not a policy says so. The policy that works is not the longest one. It states which data may go where, who approves a new tool, and what happens when someone gets it wrong. It does this in language a new hire reads in one sitting. ## What does a working AI acceptable use policy actually need to say? A policy that survives contact with real staff decides a short list of things, not a long one. Nine sections make up a working one. Each row here names the section, the decision it forces, and the specific failure it exists to prevent. | Section | What it decides | Failure it prevents | | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Scope | Which staff, contractors and AI tools the policy covers. | A contractor or a new hire assuming the rules do not apply to them. | | Data classification | Which data tier may reach which category of AI vendor. | Client or personal data pasted into a public chatbot with no data agreement. | | Approved tools and requests | Which AI systems are pre-approved, and how staff add another one. | Staff picking an unapproved tool because asking takes too long. | | Human review | Whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer, a contract or a filing. | An unreviewed AI draft going out under someone's name. | | Customer disclosure | When the company must tell a customer they are talking to an AI system or seeing AI-made content. | A hidden AI interaction reaching a customer where disclosure is a legal duty. | | Vendor training use | Whether a vendor may use company or client input to train its own models. | Confidential input quietly improving a vendor's public model. | | Ownership and review | Who owns the policy, and how often it is checked against what staff actually use. | A policy that describes a tool nobody uses, and stays silent about the one everyone does. | | Incident reporting | What staff do the moment an AI system produces something wrong or exposes data. | A bad output or a leak going unreported because nobody knew who to tell. | | Enforcement | What happens after a breach, and who decides. | A rule everyone knows the company never actually enforces. | The customer disclosure row is not optional once a system talks to people outside the company. Article 50 of the EU AI Act already requires a provider or a deployer to tell a person they are interacting with an AI system. It also requires labelling content the system generated, whether or not that system counts as high-risk. A staff-facing policy has to name who checks that duty before a customer-facing AI feature ships. The policy must not leave that to whoever built the feature to remember. ## What should the policy refuse to try to do? A policy that tries to be the technical control fails twice. It fails once because a paragraph of text cannot stop a paste into a browser. It fails again because staff read that overreach as proof the whole document is for show. Access limits, contract terms and vendor settings do the technical work. The policy states the rule those controls exist to support. Listing every approved tool by name reads as complete on the day you publish it. It is wrong within weeks, because a new model or a new vendor account always arrives faster than a document gets updated. A policy built around named tools also implies that anything missing from the list is quietly fine, and a reviewer wants to see the opposite. An outright ban is the easiest policy to write and the least effective one to run. It does not remove the reason someone went looking for an AI tool in the first place. It just moves that search out of sight, where it is much harder to see or govern. ## What do you do about the tools staff are already using? By the time you draft a policy, some staff are already using AI without asking anyone first. That means drafting client emails in a personal chatbot account or running a browser extension nobody vetted. It also means building a habit around a coding assistant they picked themselves. That is [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai), and treating it as rare is the first mistake a policy can make. Two moves fix more of it than a warning email does. First, make the approved path faster than the workaround: a fast yes for a low-risk tool beats a slow review nobody wants to wait for. Second, check instead of asking. Checking browser extensions, expense claims and what the company actually pays AI vendors shows what people are really running. That beats trusting a self-reported survey. ## What happens when someone breaks the policy? Most breaches are not sabotage. Someone pastes a client's contract into a personal chatbot account to move faster, not to leak it. That is different from someone who was told a tool was blocked and used it anyway, or who hid AI involvement in work they signed off as their own. A policy that cannot tell the two apart will punish the wrong case or excuse the real one. One named role decides what happens next. That is the same person who owns the AI register and the policy itself, not a group chat and not a vote. They classify what happened and decide whether legal or an affected client needs to hear about it. They also choose the response, from a conversation to removal of access to company systems. That decision runs through the disciplinary process HR already has for any other policy breach. The AI policy needs a clear point where that existing process starts, not a punishment system of its own. Silence is its own answer too. If a policy never states what happens after a breach, staff test it once and learn from the result whether any of it is real. ## Who should own it, and how does it stay current? The same person who is already accountable for AI risk overall should hold this document. A shared inbox cannot hold it, because someone has to be answerable when a customer or an auditor asks a direct question. [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, reviewed on a schedule and checked against a live inventory. A review interval only works if you tie it to something that actually changes. That can be a new hire, a new vendor account, or a client contract that names a data rule of its own. Quarterly is a reasonable default for a company this size. The exact interval matters less than the fact that one exists and someone is accountable for keeping it. The version I run for my own practice is public at [my AI policy](/ai-policy). It is one page, a worked example of the same shape at a much smaller scale. The [Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) lists the documents a security review asks for and who signs each. It suits a company with more than one person to coordinate. ## What doesn't a policy like this solve? A written policy does not tell you whether anyone inside the company actually owns AI risk today. If nobody does, there is no obvious person to hand the draft to. So the gap usually surfaces during an [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment), before it ever reaches the policy stage. Someone determined to break the rule will do it regardless; no policy stops that. A policy removes the excuse of not knowing, and it gives the company a fair, defensible reason to act when someone crosses the line anyway. Nobody enforces it without an owner, a review date and a stated consequence. Skip those and it is a page people skim once and never open again.

rows.text: Evals in CI put a fixed test set on every prompt, model, or code change. The build fails when the pass rate drops. A regression gets caught before a reviewer approves the pull request, not after a customer notices. Build the set from real production traffic. Sample across a period long enough that one quiet week does not flatter the result. Most agent tasks have no single correct answer. Score them in layers instead. Start with deterministic checks: a tool call shape, a required field, a data format. Add a reference-free judge for whether an answer is grounded in what the agent retrieved. Fall back to a comparison against the last known-good version for everything else. Treat the judge as a component that needs calibration against a human-labelled sample, not as ground truth. rows.text: An eval suite that only runs on a laptop protects nobody. The same regression a developer catches by eye on a good day slips through on a bad one. A model provider's silent update slips through every time. Putting [an eval suite](/glossary/evals) in CI turns a habit into a gate. The pull request cannot merge until the numbers clear, whoever is watching. ## How do you build an eval set from production traffic? Pull the first cases from what the agent has actually handled, not from what a spec said it should handle. Real traces carry the phrasing, the edge cases, and the odd multi-step requests. A person writing test data from imagination never thinks to include them. A support agent's eval set should read like a week of its own transcripts, because that is exactly what it is. Sample across a period long enough that one good or bad week does not decide the result. On only.help, my own product, the support-triage rollout built its first eval set from tickets already answered. It then found that the [first week looked better than the system really was](/case-studies/only-help-agentic-support), purely from seasonal timing. A month of traffic spans weekdays, weekends, and spikes the business already expects, which is a sturdier base than one convenient week. Mix the set on purpose. Include three kinds of case: routine ones that should always pass, a handful known to be hard, and a few with no single acceptable answer. Most agent tasks in production fall into that last kind. Store the set next to the code it tests, in a format a reviewer can read in a pull request. Change it through the same review a code change gets. Revisit the set on a fixed schedule rather than whenever someone remembers. Retire a case once the product has genuinely outgrown it. Add one the day a new failure reaches production. That keeps the set tracking how people actually use the agent. ## How do you score an agent when there is no golden answer? Most agent tasks do not reduce to one correct string, so do not force them into that shape. A support reply, a summary, or a multi-step tool sequence can be right in more than one way. A scorer built for exact match will reject good answers as often as it catches bad ones. Score in layers instead, cheapest and most reliable checks first. Start with deterministic checks on anything mechanical. Check whether the agent called the right tool, with a valid argument set, in a shape that downstream code can actually parse. These checks are cheap, and they never disagree with themselves. In most agentic systems, they catch a large share of regressions before a judge ever runs. OWASP's list of risks in large language model applications names excessive agency as one of the standard failure modes worth testing for. Excessive agency means an agent taking an action its task never asked for. Write a case for every tool the agent can call. Each case should check that the tool stays quiet when not needed, and that it fires correctly when needed. For the answer's content, add a reference-free judge. Look at the question and whatever the agent actually retrieved. Then check whether every claim in the answer traces back to a document it had in hand. This catches a fluent, confident answer that is not supported by anything the system looked at. A plain accuracy score misses that failure mode entirely. Where no rubric fits cleanly, fall back to a comparison against the last known-good version. Show a judge both outputs, blind to which one is new, and ask it to pick a winner. A judge finds picking a winner easier than defending an absolute score out of some invented scale. A win rate against a fixed baseline is also a steadier number to watch than a score with no anchor. NIST's AI RMF frames this as a selection problem under its Measure function. Which method fits depends on what is actually being measured. A team documents why it chose a metric, and which ones it rejected. That team ends up with a sturdier suite than one that picked whatever was easiest to compute. ## What happens when the judge itself is flaky? A judge model can score the same input differently on two runs, especially at a higher temperature. That alone will make a pipeline look unstable, even when the agent under test has not changed. Set the judge's own temperature as low as the provider allows. Treat any remaining run-to-run disagreement as a property of the judge to manage. Calibrate the judge on a fixed schedule against a small set of cases a human has already scored. The number that matters is agreement between the judge and the human reviewers. A judge that is consistent but consistently wrong is worse than one that is honestly uncertain. Consistent wrongness hides the problem instead of showing it. Let the judge decline a case it cannot confidently assess. A skipped case should fall out of the pass-rate calculation, rather than count as either a pass or a fail. A case the judge skips often is telling you the rubric does not cover that situation yet. When one specific case flips between pass and fail on identical re-runs, treat that case as broken, not the whole gate. Quarantine it. Keep it running so you can see it, stop it from blocking a merge, and put a name against fixing its rubric or its sampling. Only then should it rejoin the set that actually gates a build. ## What should the pipeline check, and what does a failing check do to the build? Not every check should carry the same weight. A wrong tool call and a slow response are both real problems, but only one of them should stop a release. The table below is the shape of a working gate. It shows what each row measures, how it gets a number, and what that number does to the build when it fails. | What to score | How to score it | What a failing score does to the build | | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Task success on labelled cases | Exact match or a deterministic rule against a known-good answer. | Blocks the merge immediately, with no override. | | Task success with no golden answer | A rubric-based judge scores the answer against stated criteria, not against a reference. | Blocks the merge once the pass rate drops below the floor set for that task. | | Faithfulness to retrieved context | A reference-free judge checks whether each claim traces back to a document the agent actually retrieved. | Blocks the merge; an unsupported claim counts as a defect, not a style note. | | Preference against the last good version | Pairwise comparison: the judge sees both outputs, blind to which is new, and picks a winner. | Blocks the merge if the new version loses on more cases than the agreed margin allows. | | Tool-call correctness | Deterministic check that the agent called the right tool with a valid, schema-checked argument set. | Blocks the merge; a malformed call fails loudly instead of degrading quietly. | | Judge-human agreement | Re-run the rubric against a human-labelled sample on a fixed schedule and compare agreement. | Does not block a single pull request; a drop pages the eval owner to fix the rubric. | | Cost per completed run | Sum of model and tool cost across the eval set, divided by cases completed. | Blocks the merge once the run exceeds the ceiling set in the pipeline config. | | Response time under load | Wall-clock time per case, measured in the same job as the scores. | Warns on the pull request; blocks only if it breaches the budget agreed with the product owner. | ## Where does the cost ceiling sit? Put a cost ceiling in the same job as the quality score. Do not put it on a separate dashboard someone checks once a week. Agent systems fail commercially long before they fail technically. Consider a tool call that retries a few times on a bad response: harmless in a demo, ruinous once real traffic hits it. Measure cost per completed run, across the whole eval set, the way you measure the pass rate. A change that makes the agent slower or more expensive without a real gain is a regression, even if every other score stays green. A [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) puts this gate in place before a workflow takes its first real user. That is a cheaper time to find the problem than after the first invoice. ## What does the pipeline do when a check fails? A failing check blocks the merge by default. The pull request gets a summary next to the diff that caused it. That summary lists which cases failed, what the agent returned, and what the check expected. Nobody reconstructs the failure from a log. Not every failure deserves the same response. A wrong tool call or an unsupported claim should stop the release outright. A latency or cost warning close to its budget, or a drop in judge-human agreement, can page an owner instead, without stopping every other change in the queue. Keep that distinction explicit in the pipeline config, not in someone's memory of which checks are actually load-bearing. Only a named reviewer, not the author of the change, can override a hard block. That override has to write itself into the same log the eval results live in. An override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from no gate at all. It gets used that way the next time someone is in a hurry.

rows.text: An outside AI lead sets up governance or ships a first system. Sooner or later the role has to sit with someone on the payroll. Four questions run through a handover: what moves, who takes the role, who signs what, and how the company knows it worked. ## Is there a standard way to hand over AI leadership? None turned up. In October 2026, searches of standards bodies, regulators and journals found no standard, law or study on this exact move. What exists sits next door. Interim and fractional executives have exit practices. Engineering teams have ways to transfer ownership of a service. A UK financial regulator has rules for handing over a senior role. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) and the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) texts checked in October 2026 never mention a change of person. The evidence is thin. [One academic model of interim assignments](https://doi.org/10.1108/JOEPP-10-2019-0094) says the evidence base on interim effectiveness lacks empirical studies. A company linked to two of its authors funded its literature search. Most checklists come from firms that sell interim or fractional staff. Read what follows as practice that others found sensible, plus some points that have no outside source. None of it is proven. ## What has to move in a handover? Documents alone can fall short. [Esya](https://esya.studio/notes/ai-evals-runbook-handover), a UK studio that builds AI inside client companies, writes that a folder of documents can be complete while the handover is not. It says the receiving team also needs the route to deploy and controlled access to systems. It needs monitoring data, the [evals](/glossary/evals) and the runbook. It needs authority over incidents and practised knowledge. Esya sells related work, so read that as a peer's view. The table shows what each source asks for, and how much weight it can bear. Six rows come from sources about handovers, exits or onboarding. The three NIST rows are marked. The NIST text checked in October 2026 never mentions a change of person, so applying it to a handover is this page's reading. | What moves | What a source asks for | The source and its weight | | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Decisions and reasons. | Handover material should include judgement and opinion, not just facts and figures. | [UK Financial Conduct Authority handbook](https://handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/sysc25/sysc25s9). Regulator guidance for UK financial firms, so an analogy only. | | Work in progress. | A status report on the goals set at the start: what got done, what remains and what new issues emerged. | [CompassPoint](https://www.compasspoint.org/sites/default/files/documents/Interim%20EDs%20-%20final.pdf). A practitioner's guide to interim directors of US nonprofits. | | The list of AI systems. | Mechanisms to inventory AI systems. | [NIST AI RMF](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/), Govern 1.6. A voluntary framework that NIST says it is revising. Not about handovers: this row is the page's reading. | | Roles and authority. | Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication for mapping, measuring and managing AI risks are documented and clear to individuals and teams throughout the organisation. | NIST AI RMF, Govern 2.1. Voluntary. Not about handovers: this row is the page's reading. | | How to run and change the system. | The route to deploy, monitoring data, the evals, a runbook and authority over incidents. | Esya. A studio that sells related work. | | Access. | Revoke access in one coordinated step on or before the last day, and confirm it in writing. | [Fractionus](https://fractionus.com/blog/fractional-executive-offboarding). A marketplace that sells fractional executives, so one vendor's opinion. | | Monitoring and incident duty. | Monitoring plans that cover incident response, recovery and change management. | NIST AI RMF, Manage 4.1. Voluntary. Not about handovers: this row is the page's reading. | | Someone to ask. | The development team must be available to back up and advise the receiving team while it settles. | [Google's SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/evolving-sre-engagement-model/). The operator's own account of its engineering teams. | | A report on how it went. | An exit review that names the issues the client needs to address. | [Institute of Interim Management code](https://iim.org.uk/resources/code-of-conduct/). A professional body's code for UK interim managers. | Nine rows are a lot to move on one day. Google's book describes a progressive transfer of responsibilities and ownership, including parts of operations, the change management process and access rights. This page reads that as support for moving a handover in steps. ## Who should take the role? The company side needs one named person with the authority to pause the system. The [pilot article](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) says the same. It adds that the person should have written at least one eval case and watched a rollback rehearsal. Someone who was not part of the build inherits a document, not an understanding. This site's own pages point to two jobs inside the role. rows.text: A security review of an AI system usually starts with one question: what is actually running. If the honest answer takes a week of digging through chat logs and old tickets, the review stalls before it reaches architecture or data flows. An AI system register is the fix: one document listing every AI system a company runs, who owns it, and how risky it is. ## What is an AI system register? An AI system register is the full inventory of every AI system a company runs, regardless of how it got there. That includes a customer-facing feature and an internal copilot. It also includes a marketing tool with a model switched on inside it that nobody called an AI project when they signed up. A working entry names what the system does, what data can reach it, and which vendor or model sits behind it. It also names who owns it and a rough risk tier. Some call this same list an [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) rather than an AI system register. Most of the systems on the list never started as a formal AI project. That is why the list has to go looking for them rather than wait to be told. ## Why does a security reviewer ask for it before anything else? A security or procurement reviewer asks one version of the same question first: what touches our data. Without a register, answering that means paging engineering, marketing, finance and support one by one, and hoping nobody forgot a tool. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) treats this as a named control, not a nice extra. Its Govern function includes a specific requirement: a mechanism to inventory AI systems, resourced according to how much risk the organisation is willing to carry. Everything a reviewer asks next, a data flow diagram, a vendor contract clause, an incident plan, gets scoped against rows already on this list. Skip the register, and the reviewer either stalls the process or signs off on a system nobody can fully describe. ## What should the register record? A register only earns its keep if a reviewer can answer their own questions from it, without a follow-up meeting. What follows is close to the version I hand a client. It has enough fields to answer a first review, and no field that exists only to look thorough. | What to record | Why a reviewer wants it | Who fills it in | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Name the system and what it does. | A reviewer cannot scope a check against a system they cannot picture. | The system's product or engineering owner. | | Note whether the company built it in-house or bought it, and which vendor or model sits behind it. | A vendor's own controls become part of the risk the moment its API touches your data. | Whoever set up the account or the integration. | | List the data the system can see. | This sets the risk tier and decides which contract terms and legal duties actually apply. | The team that owns the data source, with legal signing off. | | Record who relies on the system's output. | Blast radius matters as much as data sensitivity when a reviewer decides how much scrutiny to apply. | The system owner, from usage or team headcount. | | Mark its deployment status: pilot, production or retired. | A pilot running on sample data is a different conversation from a live system holding real customer records. | The system owner, kept current as status changes. | | Name one internal owner. | A reviewer wants a person who can answer for the system, not a distribution list nobody reads. | Whoever runs the team that operates the system. | | Assign a risk tier. | This decides how much documentation, testing and sign-off the reviewer expects before anything ships. | Whoever runs the security or risk review, not the system's own owner. | | Log the date it was last checked. | A register that has not moved in a year gets treated the same as no register at all. | Whoever owns the register process, on a fixed schedule. | ## How do you build one in a week without buying a tool? None of this needs procurement. A spreadsheet, a shared document and four short conversations get a usable first version out the door. - **Monday.** Create the spreadsheet with those three columns. Seed it with every system already in use: the model inside the product, the support tool, the analytics dashboard that quietly added an AI summary. - **Tuesday and Wednesday.** Interview engineering, marketing, finance and support directly, not by survey. Ask each team what they actually use day to day, since a spreadsheet plug-in with a model behind it belongs on the list too. - **Thursday.** Fill in the vendor, data and risk-tier columns from what you heard. Flag anything nobody could describe clearly for a follow-up conversation rather than a guess. - **Friday.** Assign an owner to every row, pick a reviewer for the risk tiers, and put a recheck date on the calendar before anyone calls the list finished. ## What a register does not do Building the register is the easy part of this, and several harder parts of AI governance sit outside it. It does not replace a lawyer's read of a vendor contract. The register tells legal which vendor to check and what data reaches them. It says nothing about whether that vendor's specific contract terms are safe to sign. Those terms change often enough that last year's answer will not do. The registration duty in the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) is a separate, public step for certain high-risk systems. It means registering under Article 49, in the database the Commission set up under Article 71, before the system goes live. An internal register is how you find out fast which systems might owe that separate duty; it is not a substitute for filing it. It does not stay accurate on its own, either. A register nobody owns drifts out of date within a quarter, and a stale register reads to a reviewer as no register at all. If you would rather someone else run the discovery and the first risk pass, an [AI Readiness & Risk Assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) does the same work in two weeks. It also hands you a finished register. The [starter kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) lists the register with the other documents a security review asks for.
