rows.text: This page starts from what is required, then asks what the evidence supports. The [AI operating model](/glossary/ai-operating-model) here is the one the glossary defines. What the law requires about structure is narrow, and the dates are still moving. What the evidence supports is long and weak. ## Does any law require an AI committee or a Chief AI Officer? For a private company, no source reviewed for this page requires any of four things. They are a committee, a centre of excellence, a hub-and-spoke model and a Chief AI Officer. The European Commission's [AI literacy Q&A](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers) asks whether an AI officer is necessary, as under the GDPR. It also asks whether an organisation must set up an [AI governance](/glossary/ai-governance) board. The answer is "No, no specific governance structure is mandated to comply with article 4 of the AI Act." That answer covers Article 4 only. The one binding rule found for this page that does require such structures is American. [OMB's memo on federal AI use](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-21-Accelerating-Federal-Use-of-AI-through-Innovation-Governance-and-Public-Trust.pdf), dated 3 April 2025, tells each federal agency to name a Chief AI Officer. Each agency covered by the CFO Act must also convene an AI governance board. Even there, agencies "are permitted to rely on existing governance bodies." The memo binds US federal agencies and nobody else. The standards read the same way. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) is voluntary. Its [published text](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/nist.ai.100-1.pdf) calls it "use-case agnostic, providing flexibility to organizations of all sizes." It prescribes no committee or team shape. [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) applies to "any organization, regardless of size." Its contents list roles, responsibilities and authorities. The standard is sold, not published, so its clause text was not read for this page. ## What does the law require instead? In the Articles reviewed here, the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) asks for duties, not structures. Which duties apply depends on what a company does with AI. It also depends on whether the company is the [provider or the deployer](/glossary/provider-vs-deployer) of each system. The table lists the duties of the Articles reviewed, by trigger, using the [consolidated text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng). The [Digital Omnibus](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, rewrote some of the wording and moved the dates in July 2026. The last column is a reading of what each duty needs in practice. It is not law text. | If your company… | The duty | Applies from | What it needs in practice | | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Provides or deploys any AI system | Article 4: take measures to support the AI literacy of staff and others who use AI for you. No specific level is required. | In application since 2 February 2025. National authorities enforce from 2 August 2026. | Someone to run the measures. The Commission says there is no need for a certificate and that organisations can keep an internal record of trainings. | | Runs a chatbot or generates synthetic content | Article 50: transparency duties for providers and deployers of chatbots, generative systems and deepfake content. Providers of generative systems must mark outputs in a machine-readable format. | 2 August 2026. Generative systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to mark. | An owner for disclosure wording, and for marking if you provide the system. | | Provides a [high-risk AI system](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system) | Article 17: a documented quality management system with an accountability framework. It sets out the responsibilities of management and other staff. It must fit the size of the provider. | 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems. 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. | A written accountability framework. | | Deploys a high-risk AI system | Article 26: give [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) to people with "the necessary competence, training and authority". Also monitor the system, keep logs for six months or more, and report risks. | The same two dates. | Named overseers. The Act leaves the deployer "freedom to organise its own resources and activities". | | Changes a system someone else built | Article 25: a deployer becomes the provider if it puts its own name on a high-risk system or changes it substantially. The same happens if it changes a system's purpose so that it becomes high-risk. | No start date for Article 25 in the sources reviewed. | A change-control step that decides when the role flips. | Look at what these duties name. They name an accountability framework (Article 17) and people with the competence, training and authority for human oversight (Article 26). None names a committee, a centre of excellence or a Chief AI Officer. In practice, Article 4 needs someone to run the literacy measures and Article 50 needs an owner for disclosure wording; that is a reading, not law text. The Commission adds that, for deployers of high-risk systems, the duty to train staff for human oversight "remains in place" alongside Article 4. ### How firm are the EU dates? The omnibus was signed on 8 July 2026 and is in force from 27 July. It moved the high-risk dates to 2 December 2027 (Annex III systems) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I systems). Its preamble gives the reason: "the delayed availability of standards, common specifications, and alternative guidance and the delayed establishment of national competent authorities." It also rewrote Article 4 and Article 17(2). Treat the new dates with care. The omnibus dates from July 2026, and several Commission guidelines are still pending, so the practical detail is still to come. Company size also changes the exposure to fines. Small and medium-sized companies pay the lower of the two fine limits. The omnibus extends that rule to small mid-cap companies, a new size class just above them, for all but the highest tier. ## Who decides, and who answers? This page treats five decisions as ones that need a named owner; that is the writer's reading, not a finding of any source. The table sets what law and standards say about each against what surveys report. The last table in the next section gives the sample behind each survey. | Decision | What law and standards say | What organisations report | | ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Approve a system for production | NIST asks executive leadership to take responsibility for decisions about AI risk (GOVERN 2.3). It prescribes no committee or team shape. | The Bank of England and FCA surveyed 118 firms in 2024. 72% give accountability for AI use cases to executive leadership. Most name three or more accountable people or bodies. | | Own the evaluation | NIST MEASURE 1.3: internal experts who did not build the system, or independent assessors, join regular assessments. | No source reviewed says who should own an evaluation set after handover at a company of this size. | | Sign risk acceptance | NIST asks for residual risk to be documented. It names no signer, and neither do the AI Act articles reviewed. | The US federal memo names one: a waiver of its requirements for high-impact AI needs a written determination by the agency's Chief AI Officer. | | Keep the inventory | NIST GOVERN 1.6 asks for mechanisms to inventory AI systems. | ASIC found some licensees with no AI inventory and others with several dispersed model registers. | | Run it after launch | AI Act Article 26: deployers of high-risk systems monitor them, keep logs for six months or more and report risks. | A 2025 survey sponsored by Pacific AI found that 48% of organisations monitor production AI systems. It gives no clear figure for companies of this size. | In the table, NIST speaks to four of these decisions and AI Act Article 26 to the fifth. Of the texts reviewed, no NIST subcategory names an approver, NIST names no risk-acceptance signer and the AI Act articles reviewed name none. Practice varies too. The IAPP and Credo AI report says: "There is no clear best practice for how to build and organize an AI governance team." ASIC describes better and poorer practice for a committee where one exists. It describes better practice as a cross-functional, executive-level committee with clear responsibility and decision-making authority. Poorer practice was a committee that met infrequently and had a poorly defined mandate. Fewer than a third of the licensees it reviewed had a committee, or were setting one up. The [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) is where the owner and risk tier of each system live, and a short review checklist can be attached to each entry. The [register post](/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-system-register-in-a-week) shows how to keep one. ## Which structures do companies use, and how good is the evidence? Each structure in this table carries a grade in plain words. Required means a law or binding rule says it. Observed means a regulator or a survey reports what organisations do, with the sample named. Recommended means a research centre, a consultancy or a vendor says organisations should. Popular means many vendors repeat it and no data was found behind it. Described, not evaluated means an arrangement is described and no effect is reported. | Structure | What it means | What the evidence is | Grade | | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Centralised | One team or centre of excellence decides, and often builds. | [Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-30-gartner-survey-finds-forty-five-percent-of-organizations-with-high-artificial-intelligence-maturity-keep-artificial-intelligence-projects-operational-for-at-least-three-years) reports that almost 60% of high-maturity organisations centralise AI strategy, governance, data and infrastructure. | Observed. Gartner scores maturity from a seven-question survey; its press release does not list the questions. | | Hub-and-spoke or federated | A central group sets standards. Units run the work. | [McKinsey's guide](https://www.hkdca.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/data-leaders-operating-guide-scaling-ai-mckinsey.pdf) describes three archetypes: centralised, federated and decentralised, with a trade-off for each, and says the decentralised one needs very high domain maturity and sufficient scale. [IBM](https://www.ibm.com/thought-leadership/institute-business-value/en-us/report/chief-ai-officer) surveyed Chief AI Officers. Those leading hub-and-spoke or centralised models report twice as many pilots moved into production and 36% higher ROI. Every respondent was a Chief AI Officer, so each already had a central AI leader. IBM adds that organisations generally move from decentralised models to centralised or hub-and-spoke models as they scale. [Microsoft](https://blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2021/01/19/microsoft-responsible-ai-program/) describes its own hub and spokes. It is the one long-running named case, and it is a very large company describing itself. | Observed and recommended. The ROI is self-reported. No cost or failure data. | | Decentralised | Each unit owns its own AI work. | [ASIC](https://download.asic.gov.au/media/mtllqjo0/rep-798-published-29-october-2024.pdf) placed its "leveraged, decentralised" licensees in the middle of its maturity scale. [MIT NANDA](https://cloudelligent.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/v0.1_State_of_AI_in_Business_2025_Report.pdf) found that decentralised implementation works when accountability stays put: "companies succeed when they decentralize implementation authority but retain accountability." | Observed. The sources point different ways. | | Embedded | AI people sit inside business units. | One case story from [MIT CISR](https://cisr.mit.edu/publication/2025_0801_EnterpriseAIMaturityUpdate_WoernerSebastianWeillKaganer): Italgas placed business translators in each unit and added a group AI office. No source reviewed measures this against the others or separates it from decentralised. | Popular. It shows what advisers agree on, not outcomes. | Most surveys are self-reported and lean toward large companies. ASIC's data is from December 2023. The sources also disagree about where authority should sit. IBM and Gartner lean central. MIT NANDA leans local for implementation. They may describe different layers: central for policy and risk, local for finding use cases. No source tests that reading. ## Where do the switch-point numbers come from? Vendor pages tell readers to change structure at a set number of AI projects or business units. The numbers differ from page to page. No data was found behind any of them: the one vendor page read in full cites no data for its numbers, and the other two were seen only as search snippets. One page also puts a figure on rework. That figure has no data behind it either. This page does not repeat those numbers. Printing a number gives it weight the evidence does not give it. The three vendor thresholds found have no data behind them. No source reviewed reports a cost for any structure in headcount, budget or time. One ASIC finding is about the order of events. In that sample, most governance uplifts were still being planned or started when the licensees expected their use of AI to rise. ## What fits a company of 30 to 300 people? Small companies were far less likely than larger ones to have a role or office for AI governance. Pacific AI sponsored it. Small there includes companies under 30 people. The [UTS Human Technology Institute](https://www.uts.edu.au/research/centres/human-technology-institute/projects/ai-corporate-governance-program/ai-governance-snapshot-series/contentassets/designing-ai-governance-structures.pdf) describes a lean design: "a single accountable executive supported by a small cross-functional working group." It says the CEO may take that role in a smaller organisation. It also says "There is not a single correct answer to these questions." Its papers show what advisers agree on, not what has been shown to work. Parts of the law scale with size too. Article 17(2) ties a provider's quality management system to the size of its organisation. The Australian government's [AI adoption guidance](https://www.ai.gov.au/staying-safe-and-responsible/essential-ai-practices/guidance-ai-adoption-foundations) tells organisations to adapt each practice to their size. It also asks for a senior leader as the overall owner and a specific person accountable for every system. ## How do you choose? The evidence cannot pick a structure for you. It can narrow the choice. What follows is a reading of the sources, not a finding from any of them. 1. Start from the duties you have. Decide for each AI system whether your company is the provider or the deployer, and whether the system is high-risk. That decides which dates apply. 2. Name an owner for each of the five decisions. The law and the standards reviewed ask for named people with clear roles. None requires a committee. 3. Choose the smallest structure that covers them. The lean design above is one accountable executive and a small working group. Add a standing group only when a decision needs more than one function. Give any group a clear mandate and regular meetings, because ASIC's poorer practice was a committee that met infrequently and had a poorly defined mandate. 4. Pick triggers from your own events, not from a vendor number. Review the structure when a duty date arrives, when you add a high-risk system, after an incident, or when use grows faster than the controls. 5. Test the structure on your own records at a fixed date. None of the large studies reports results for a company your size. Your register does. The [post on why pilots stall](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) shows what happens when step two is skipped. Write the five names down first. Then see whether any duty above needs more than that. ## What do these sources leave out? They cannot say which structure produces better results at a company this size. None of the large studies reports results for companies of 30 to 300 people. They give no cost for any structure. Most are dated 2023 to 2026; Microsoft's account of its own programme is from 2021, and two pages carry no date. Some of the data is older than the omnibus. Agentic systems are a gap. No regulator text or standard reviewed assigns decision rights to an AI agent. The Australian guidance still says to name a person accountable for every system. Standards are moving too. NIST says its framework "is being updated", so every subcategory cited here comes from the January 2023 text.

rows.text: Microsoft, Google Cloud and AWS each publish guidance on multi-agent systems. The guidance is useful, and it agrees on more than you might expect. It is also vendor guidance with little measured evidence behind it. In my reading it says least about limits, rollback and ownership. This page grades the main claims and says plainly where the research found nothing. A multi-agent system, in these sources, puts several agents on one task. Each agent is a model with its own instructions and tools. One agent usually coordinates the rest. The sources call it an orchestrator, a supervisor, a coordinator, a manager agent or a lead agent. This page says orchestrator. The [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow) entry in the glossary covers the wider idea. Outside claims name their source, and a date where the page has one. I read each page on 2 October 2026, except the Gartner release. Gartner blocks scripted reads, so I checked its sentences on a reproduction. Several of the pages change often. Where I write that I found no source, I mean none among the sources I read. A miss does not prove nobody says it elsewhere. ## How far can each claim be trusted? Treat most of it as advice. Almost none of it was measured in a production workload. The table grades the points that matter most, and the sections after it give the detail. | Point | What the sources show | How far to trust it | | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | One agent or several | Anthropic (13 June 2025) reports gains from its multi-agent research system. Cognition (12 June 2025) argued against agents working together. On 22 April 2026 it said its observations still hold for parallel writers. | Each is one vendor's own work. I found no source that compares both in a production workload. | | Test failure rates | A NeurIPS 2025 paper (revised 26 October 2025) found failure rates from 41% to 86.7% across seven open-source frameworks. | Peer reviewed. It tested open-source frameworks, not production systems with an eval gate. | | Cancelled projects | Gartner (25 June 2025) forecasts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. | A forecast. The release leans on a poll of 3,412 webinar attendees. | | Runaway loops | Anthropic says early versions spawned 50 subagents for simple queries. A preprint (2 July 2026) found loop-prone code in 47 projects. | Not found: a dated post-mortem from production. The only accounts found repeat one set of figures with no primary record. | | Human approval | Anthropic (25 May 2026) says users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts. Microsoft (4 June 2026) calls bypass of the human step the most consistently exploited failure mode. | Each is the vendor's own finding. Anthropic's post gives no method for its figure. | | Evals in CI | Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework (3 December 2025) and Anthropic's evals post (9 January 2026) say to run evaluations in CI/CD pipelines. | Two primary sources among the pages searched. A practice, not a standard. | | Rollback speed | Microsoft says "immediate". Temporal says "instant". | Not found: a target time in any source reviewed. | ## Do the big vendors agree on a shape? My reading is mostly yes, on four ideas. A coordinating agent routes work to others. Tool access goes through one controlled boundary. State lives outside the model. Every call is logged against a named identity. The guides do not all say all four, but each idea recurs. Microsoft's [reference architecture](https://microsoft.github.io/multi-agent-reference-architecture/docs/reference-architecture/Reference-Architecture.html), last updated on 18 August 2025, has an orchestrator. It consults a classifier to route a request and a registry to find agents. It connects tools through a [Model Context Protocol](/glossary/mcp) server and keeps state in persistent storage. The [multi-agent guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/multiagent-ai-system) from Google Cloud, last reviewed on 16 September 2025, also centres on a coordinator agent. Microsoft, Google Cloud and Anthropic each advise starting small. Microsoft (12 February 2026) says to use the lowest level of complexity that reliably meets your requirements. Google Cloud (reviewed 28 May 2026) recommends starting with a single agent if you are early in agent development. Anthropic (19 December 2024, updated 10 August 2026) advises finding the simplest solution possible and adding complexity only when needed. AWS (10 June 2026) warns of coordination overhead, handoff complexity and distributed failure modes. An undated AWS Marketplace learning module, written in the first person, also recommends the simplest pattern that fits your workflow. These are companies that sell the platforms. The Microsoft and Google Cloud pages quoted above report no measured data. Their agreement tells you what the vendors advise. ## Should the default be one agent or several? Start with one. Microsoft, Google Cloud and Anthropic each advise starting small, and the sources still disagree about what comes next. Two of the sources landed a day apart, and my reading is that they disagree on where the line sits. Cognition, which makes the Devin coding agent, published ["Don't Build Multi-Agents"](https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents) on 12 June 2025. Anthropic described its [multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) on 13 June 2025. Cognition wrote that "in 2025, running multiple agents in collaboration only results in fragile systems." One of its principles was to share context. Anthropic says its research system "uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern". A lead agent coordinates specialised subagents that run in parallel. Anthropic's own evaluations show that such systems "excel especially for breadth-first queries". I read that as a read-heavy task, graded by the vendor itself. Cognition came back to the question on 22 April 2026. Its original observations, it wrote, "still hold today for parallel-writer swarms". It also described a narrower pattern that works, in which several agents add intelligence to a task while "writes stay single-threaded". The same post gives two rules that pull apart. One says to "share as much context as possible between the agents". For review agents, it says the technique works best when the coding and review agents "do not share any context beforehand". I would expect the line to fall between reading and writing. Many independent reads suit several agents. Writes that must agree suit one. I found no source that tested that expectation in a production workload, so treat it as a working rule. The closest measurement found is a Google Research study of agent designs on benchmark tasks. Its [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296), posted on 9 December 2025 and revised on 8 April 2026, compared several designs with a single agent. Results ran from a gain of 80.8% to a loss of 70.0%, depending on the task. The Google Research blog post about the paper, of 28 January 2026, reports that independent agents amplified errors 17.2 times, and centralised ones 4.4 times. The blog counts fewer test configurations than the paper's latest abstract, so the paper changed after the blog. I cannot say the multipliers hold for the paper. Anthropic's own post says multi-agent systems "work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem". One reading is that more tokens help, however they are spent. I found no source that separates the gain from structure from the gain from extra tokens. ## What do the failure studies show? Multi-agent systems fail often in tests, and the studies below do not show how often they fail in production. One is MAST, from Cemri and colleagues, accepted to the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track. It read the traces of seven open-source multi-agent frameworks and found [failure rates from 41% to 86.7%](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13657). Repeated steps and agents that miss a finished task were among the common failures. The paper is peer reviewed. It tested open-source frameworks, not production systems with an eval gate in front of them. A runaway loop is a different case, because it costs money. The research found no dated, checkable post-mortem of one in production. The only accounts I found were blog posts that repeat one set of figures with no primary record. What I found is weaker. Anthropic says early versions of its research system made errors such as spawning 50 subagents for simple queries. A [preprint of 2 July 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01641), "When Agents Do Not Stop", scanned public agent repositories for code that can start an infinite loop. It counts code patterns and does not show a loop that ran in production. Hijacking is another documented failure. NIST's CAISI tested agent hijacking on a public benchmark. The strongest new attack succeeded 81% of the time, against 11% for the strongest baseline attack. [NIST published the result](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/01/technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations) on 17 January 2025 and updated it on 19 December 2025. That is a benchmark, so it shows what is possible. It gives no rate for real systems. NIST's wording is that many agents that read untrusted text are open to [prompt injection](/glossary/prompt-injection). ## Where do limits and cost controls belong? On every run, set by a person, with a defined result when the limit is reached. The defaults in popular frameworks differ, and they count different things. The table shows five frameworks as read on 2 October 2026. The OpenAI default comes from its source code on GitHub, and the other rows from documentation pages. | Framework | Default loop limit | What it counts | | ---------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | OpenAI Agents SDK | 10 | Turns of the agent loop in one run. Setting none removes the limit. | | LangGraph | 1,000 | Steps, since version 1.0.6. | | Microsoft Agent Framework | 100 | Iterations of a workflow run toward convergence. | | Google Agent Development Kit | None stated | A loop agent ends on a stop signal or on a maximum you set. | | Claude Agent SDK | No limit unless set | The docs advise setting a budget for production agents. | A turn, a step and an iteration are different units, so in my reading the three numbers cannot be compared. Step limits and cost limits are also separate controls. The Claude Agent SDK documentation says the loop runs until Claude finishes if you set no limits. It calls a budget a good default for production agents. The [FAQ on cost per outcome](/faq/how-is-cost-per-outcome-measured) gives this site's definition of the measure, and I would set a ceiling from your own traces. ## Does an agent need durable state and traces? Yes, the sources say both. State has to survive a crash, and every call needs a trace. Anthropic's [managed agents post](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents) of 8 April 2026 keeps the session log outside the process that runs the agent. Nothing in that process has to survive a crash. Temporal, which sells durable execution, says its service hands the work to another process after a crash and rebuilds the state. LangGraph's documentation says in-memory checkpoints are lost when the process restarts, and it recommends a durable checkpointer. The principle is well supported. I found no source that says every production agent needs a separate engine, and none that measures the benefit. Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework (3 December 2025) says to attribute every action to a specific agent instance and conversation ID. The OpenTelemetry conventions for agent spans were still marked as in development in the repository file read on 2 October 2026. Whether the core traces signal is stable is unconfirmed, so this page makes no claim about it. OpenAI's Agents SDK turns tracing on by default, warns that traces may capture sensitive data, and does not offer tracing under zero data retention. Anthropic (9 January 2026, updated 18 March 2026) says an eval suite makes problems visible before they reach users, and that it needs clear ownership. Running [evals](/glossary/evals) in the pipeline that ships changes is a narrower claim. Two primary sources say it: Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework and Anthropic's evals post, which calls automated evals especially useful pre-launch and in CI/CD. That source is the Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework, which says to integrate evaluations into CI/CD pipelines before production. The [post on evals in CI](/blog/evals-in-ci-for-llm-agents) is about running them without a golden answer. ## Who approves what, and who owns the system? A person should approve high-impact actions, and one named person should own the system. The sources agree on the first and say less about the second. The Model Context Protocol specification (revision 28 July 2026) says there should always be a [human in the loop](/glossary/human-in-the-loop) who can deny tool invocations. The word is "should", and the specification says the protocol cannot enforce its own security principles. AWS sorts actions into three tiers, autonomous, notify and approve, by impact and reversibility, so that not every action waits for a person. Approval is also a control that can fail. Anthropic reports that its telemetry showed users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts (25 May 2026). It adds that the more approvals a user sees, the less attention each one gets. Microsoft's [AI Red Team](/glossary/red-teaming) calls bypass of the human step the most consistently exploited failure mode (4 June 2026). Both are the vendors' own findings. Anthropic's post gives no method for its figure. This page cannot say how many prompts is too many. Access follows the same logic. Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework (page updated 26 June 2026) says agent actions must be attributable and enforceable to a unique identity. The MCP authorization specification says authorization is optional for implementations. I read that as follows: a claim of least privilege through MCP describes how someone configured it, and the protocol does not guarantee it. On ownership, Microsoft's framework says to give agent governance to the leaders who already own cloud governance, security and compliance. It also says to designate a human role accountable for approving deployments and monitoring compliance. Microsoft's reference architecture site describes a cross-functional governance committee. In my reading these fit together if the committee advises and one person decides. This site's [approach page](/approach) asks for one named person who can refuse a launch and is accountable for AI risk. The [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) names people with competence and authority too. Its [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) duties apply to [high-risk systems](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system) only. The Commission's AI Act service desk still shows the 2024 text of those articles. ## Can you roll back a multi-agent change? Microsoft's guidance says yes, if you version everything that shapes behaviour. I found no target time in the sources I read, so I cannot say how fast. Microsoft's security page for its reference architecture (updated 12 May 2025) says to version every agent's logic, prompt configuration and communication contract. It also says to enable immediate rollback to a previous version when anomalies are detected. Temporal's "Why Temporal?" page promises instant rollback, with no measurement behind the word. Pinning a model does not always pin behaviour. Anthropic's documentation says infrastructure updates occasionally produce minor differences in observable behaviour even when the model ID and weights have not changed. I read that as follows: rolling back the model ID does not always roll back behaviour. Evals run after a rollback are how you would see the difference. Providers also retire models on published schedules, so a pinned model has an end date. Anthropic and OpenAI each publish a deprecations page, and someone has to read it. ## Which claims did the research not find a source for? The research looked for each of these and did not find it. - A dated, checkable post-mortem of a production agent loop that ran away and cost real money. - Any multi-agent reference architecture from a standards body. NIST announced an AI agent standards initiative on 17 February 2026. Its page, updated on 14 August 2026, describes convenings and gap analyses, and the research found no finished NIST guidance for agents. The ISO, IEC and IEEE catalogues were not browsed, so the honest wording is "not found". - Measured results that compare one agent with several inside one company's production workload. - A target time for rollback in any source reviewed. - Support for the "four planes" model of control, execution, state and capability beyond one undated AWS Marketplace learning module, written in the first person. One figure rests on a weak source. A LangChain blog of 16 June 2025 says to start small with evals and that even about twenty examples is enough. LangChain sells agent tooling and the post is commentary, so this page does not adopt the figure. Retrieval and memory design were outside this research. The [retrieval-augmented generation](/glossary/retrieval-augmented-generation) entry covers the basics. ## Does this site commit to any of it? Yes, to five controls. The [approach page](/approach) names evals in CI, tracing, cost per outcome, a rollback path and a named owner. In my reading, the sources above back them unevenly. Tracing recurs across the guides, and a named owner is clearest in Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework. Rollback appears as a practice in three of the 14 pages I searched. Evals in CI appears in the two primary sources named above. The outside sources cover spend limits and spend per reasoning cycle or per agent, which is a different measure from cost per outcome. I found no target time for rollback in the sources I read. The FAQ on [what counts as in production](/faq/what-counts-as-in-production-for-the-90-day-sprint) gives the bar this site uses. The [only.help case study](/case-studies/only-help-agentic-support) reports tracing on every call and a per-ticket cost ceiling checked in the same CI job as the evals. Its summary also names evals in CI and a named owner. It does not say whether the workflow used one agent or several, so this page does not use it as evidence for either. For one workflow taken to production, see the [90-day production sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint).

rows.text: An AI pilot never reached production because of an organisational gap, not a technical one. A demo only has to impress the person running it. Production has to survive a change of prompt, a change of model and a change of the person who built it. It has to do that without anyone noticing except a number on a dashboard. Six conditions decide whether that gap closes. One named owner still answers for the system a year after launch. A data classification signed off by someone with authority says what a vendor may see. An outcome number moves when the system works, matched by an eval that runs in the build pipeline before every release. Tracing shows which step produced a bad answer, and a rollback fires on a threshold, not an argument. Most stalled pilots are missing the first two, and a team cannot build the rest until those exist.

rows.text: A pilot stalls in the space between working once and working every time. Most proof-of-concepts skip four things production always needs. Two of them are a named owner who still answers a year after launch and a decision about which data may leave the building. The other two are a number that says whether the system is working, and an automatic check that catches a regression before a customer does. ## Where do pilots actually stop? ### Nobody owns the risk Pilots are usually built by whoever was curious enough to try. That person is rarely still around, or still in charge, once the project needs a decision about risk. Nobody has the standing to say the system is ready, and nobody has to explain a bad output to a customer or a regulator. Ownership means one name attached to the outcome, with the budget and the authority to pause the system if it misbehaves. A shared inbox or a Slack channel does not count. Without that name, every stall becomes permanent, because nobody is accountable for unsticking it. ### Legal has not said which data may leave Most pilots reach a vendor's API before anyone has classified the data going into the prompt. That is fine for a demo running on sample records. It stops a rollout the moment a security review asks what customer data the system touches and where it goes. The NIST AI RMF treats this as a governance decision under its Govern function, not a technical detail to settle after launch. Without a data classification written down in advance, every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. The pilot waits on a decision nobody has been asked to make yet. ### There is no measurable outcome A pilot that nobody can prove is working also cannot be proven to be failing, which is worse. Teams show accuracy on a curated test set, or a handful of good transcripts. Nobody has picked the business number the system is meant to move. Examples are tickets resolved, hours saved or the error rate on a defined task. Without that number, a debate about whether to invest further has no evidence on either side. The safest move for everyone involved is to let the pilot run quietly forever, rather than kill it or fund it properly. ### Nobody would notice a regression Prompts change, the underlying model changes on a provider's own schedule, and traffic drifts. Pilots rarely have a way to detect when any of that makes the output worse. There is no test suite running against real examples before a change ships. So a regression appears first as a customer complaint or a bad downstream decision, not as a failed build. That is the opposite of how the rest of the engineering organisation ships software. This gap is usually the reason a platform or security review declines to sign off. ## What has to be true to ship? Six conditions turn a pilot into something a platform team will actually run. None of them are exotic. Most engineering teams already do the equivalent for every other production system they own. | Condition | What it means in practice | What its absence looks like | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | An owner. | One named person, on the team that runs the system, with authority to pause it. | No one can explain a bad output, so the stall becomes permanent. | | A data classification. | A written answer, agreed with whoever owns data risk, on what a vendor may store. | Every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. | | A measurable outcome. | One number the business already tracks, with a floor the system must clear. | Nobody can prove the pilot works, so it runs quietly forever instead of shipping or dying. | | Evals in CI. | Real test cases run on every prompt or model change; OWASP treats this as baseline hygiene. | A regression reaches a customer before anyone on the team sees it. | | Tracing and cost per outcome. | Every run logged well enough to reconstruct, with a cost a finance team can read. | Nobody can say what a run costs, or which step produced a bad answer. | | Rollback. | A rehearsed way to revert to the last prompt, model or version within minutes. | The team improvises during the first real incident instead of using a tested path. | For a system that touches decisions about people, the EU AI Act sets a similar bar for higher-risk uses. It requires a documented risk-management process, records that make a decision traceable and a human who can step in. Meeting the six conditions above gets most of the way there even for teams the Act does not yet cover. ## How would I sequence it? I run this as one pass, not six parallel workstreams, because the six conditions above depend on each other. You cannot set a rollback threshold before you have a measured outcome, and you cannot classify data before someone owns the decision to do it. ### Pick one process Choose a single workflow with enough volume to matter and an outcome you can measure without a survey, not five pilots running at once. An AI readiness and risk assessment is the fastest way to get that choice onto paper. Two weeks of reading the existing systems and vendor list end in a memo. The memo names an owner candidate, a first data classification and the number the process should move. ### Build it in ninety days A 90-Day Production Sprint turns that memo into a running system. Evals get written alongside the first working version, rather than bolted on at the end. Tracing and cost per outcome go live on a dashboard from week one. The rollback path gets rehearsed before real traffic arrives, not during the first incident. ### Hand it to someone who was in the room The internal owner should have written at least one eval case and watched the rollback rehearsal, so the runbook describes a system they already understand. A handover document given to someone who was not part of the build is a liability with a due date, not a transfer of knowledge. ## What this does not solve This sequence gets one process into production with the six conditions in place. Several harder governance questions stay outside it. Your risk appetite is still your call, not this sequence's. Two companies with the same pilot and the same data can reasonably choose different answers about what a vendor may see. That decision belongs to whoever owns risk at your company, not something a framework or an outside advisor can make for you. It does not replace a legal review of your contracts with model vendors. Classifying data tells your lawyers what question to ask. It does not answer whether a specific vendor's terms are acceptable, and that answer changes as vendors change their terms. The underlying model is exactly as reliable as it was before this sequence started. Evals catch regressions against the cases you thought to test. They do not catch every way a general-purpose model can fail on a case nobody wrote down. That is why the rollback path matters as much as the evals do. It does not scale to five processes at once. The sequence above is built for one workflow with one owner. Running it for a second or third process repeats the same ninety days. It does not shortcut them.

rows.text: ## What this is A panel specification for tracking how AI tools are used at work. It has eight panels. Each names the question it answers, the data source and the decision it supports. It is a page, not a dashboard file. You copy the panels into whatever tool you already run. The panels fall into three kinds. The coverage, seat and retention panels count what people did. The two survey panels count what people said. The outcome, delivery health and cost panels read what the work produced. The outcome, delivery health, cost and trust panels carry the weight, and the trust survey is read as opinion. That order is a synthesis of the sources, not a finding any of them states. The [adoption telemetry article](/blog/adoption-telemetry-measuring-if-ai-is-actually-used) gives the evidence behind it. ## The eight panels | # | Panel | Question it answers | Data source | Decision it supports | | --- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 1 | Coverage | What share of AI use at work runs through approved tools? | [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) request logs, the sign-in app list, expense lines, API bills and the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) | Which tools to approve, replace or block, and where the approved path is hard | | 2 | Paid versus active | Which paid seats see no use? | Vendor admin APIs, such as GitHub's user-management `last_activity_at` | Reclaim or reassign seats, and aim training | | 3 | Retention by team | Do people who tried a tool keep using it at 4, 8 and 12 weeks? | Gateway or vendor logs, with one written definition of active | Retrain, change the workflow or retire the tool | | 4 | Outcome per use case | Did the outcome agreed before rollout move, against a baseline or a comparison group? | The system of record for that outcome, such as ticketing, CI or your CRM, not the AI tool's own logs | Scale, fix or retire the use case | | 5 | Delivery health (engineering use cases) | Did throughput or instability get worse as use grew? | CI/CD and version control: DORA's lead time for changes, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and rework rate, plus review time | Slow or pause a rollout when instability rises | | 6 | Cost per outcome | What does one unit of the outcome cost? | Spend and the outcome count from the outcome panel, as set out in [how cost per outcome is measured](/faq/how-is-cost-per-outcome-measured) | Budget, build versus buy, and model choice | | 7 | Trust and friction pulse | Do people trust the output, rely on it, and say where it gets in the way? | A short repeated survey, using the trust and reliance items DORA publishes. The smallest-group rule applies | Training and verification effort, and tool choice | | 8 | Policy clarity | Do staff know what is expected, what is allowed and what applies to them? | The same survey, using the four AI-stance items in DORA's 2025 report | Fix how the acceptable use policy is explained | The delivery health and cost panels apply to engineering and workflow use cases. Write the outcome panel for each use case. ## Fix these definitions before you build - What counts as active. GitHub needs two active days in the trailing 28 to place a user in a usage phase. Microsoft counts a returning user as one with an action in both the current and the previous period. Choose one rule, write it on the panel and keep it. - When you check retention. The retention panel uses 4, 8 and 12 weeks. Week 4 is the first check. - The smallest group you show. Microsoft's Viva Insights needs its minimum group size set to at least five. That is a product setting. The sources read here give no legal figure for a minimum group size. Set your own and write it down. ## What stays off the dashboard - Seat count as adoption. A seat shows money spent, and GitHub keeps seat data apart from its usage reports. - Daily or weekly active users with no written definition. GitHub, Microsoft and DORA each define active differently. - Prompt counts. DORA's 2024 report, published by Google Cloud, said measuring usage frequency is "likely not as meaningful as measuring reliance". - Lines of code accepted as a success measure. GitHub calls its own lines figure directional. - Acceptance rate as a success measure. In a 2022 preprint on Copilot users it tracked how productive users said they felt. - Vendor hours saved or ROI as value. Microsoft multiplies action counts by fixed minutes and a default hourly rate. - Rankings of named people. DX, a vendor of measurement software, warns against using these metrics to judge individuals. - Prompt content. The GDPR asks for no more data than needed, and Claude Code's documentation says prompt text is off by default. ## Who sees what Show team-level figures by default. Where you control the collector, filter or redact the person field before data reaches the dashboard. Claude Code includes the signed-in user's email by default, and its documentation says to filter it at your own backend if that is a concern. The paid versus active panel shows idle seats by team. Reclaiming a seat needs a name, and a name is person-level data. Write down the purpose, who sees the list and how long you keep it. Then run the screening in the [adoption telemetry article](/blog/adoption-telemetry-measuring-if-ai-is-actually-used) before the list exists. ## What it is not It is not a live dashboard, and it is not an export for one tool. It does not show that an AI tool works. Only the outcome panel can do that, against a baseline or a comparison group, and that is a synthesis, not a finding any source states. It is a summary of public documents, not legal advice.

rows.text: ## What this is A CI workflow and an eval case format for one [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow). The same discipline sits inside the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint). A prompt or model change should not merge without passing a test set first. ## The eval case format | Field | Purpose | Example | | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | id | A stable name, so a failure is traceable across runs | refund-double-charge | | input | The exact prompt or tool call the agent receives | Customer says they were charged twice | | expected | A pass rule: an exact match, a check, or a second model acting as a grader | Refund issued, ticket closed, no invented apology | | tags | The failure mode a case guards against | prompt-injection, tool-misuse, refusal | ## The CI gate The workflow runs the eval set on every pull request, scores it, and blocks the merge under your floor. Nobody has to remember to run it by hand, which is the part that fails first once a team is busy. The tags borrow their shape from [OWASP's Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/). Prompt injection and excessive agency (the agent doing something nobody asked it to) appear in a support agent as often as in a public chatbot. A tagged case catches the regression either way. ## What it is not It is not a considered eval set on its own. A handful of cases pulled from real conversations tests more than a long list invented at a desk. The starter takes no position on which cases you pick. Choosing the cases still maps to the MEASURE function (one of the framework's four functions) in [NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework).

rows.text: ## What this is The four documents that answer most of a corporate security review. They are deliberately short: a register nobody updates is worse than no register. The kit also sets out the order in which to call people when an AI system fails. ## What it is not It is not a compliance certificate, and it is not legal advice. It is the paperwork a reviewer expects to see before they look at your architecture. ## Who signs what | Document | What it's for | Who signs it | | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | AI register | Every AI system in use, who owns it, what data reaches it. | The named AI risk owner keeps it current. | | Acceptable-use policy | What you may paste into a tool, and what you may not. | Every employee who uses an AI tool for work. | | Data classification table | Which vendors may see which tier of data. | The AI risk owner, together with whoever owns the data. | | Vendor questionnaire | One answer set procurement can reuse for every new vendor. | Procurement, before anyone signs a vendor contract. | It maps loosely to what ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) both expect a company to have on file. It does not require either. ## Vendor questionnaire The other three documents describe how you handle AI. This one asks each vendor how it handles your data. Send the same questions to every AI vendor, and file the answers with the contract. The questions cover these topics: - Whether the vendor trains models on your data, and how you opt out. - Where your data is processed and stored, who at the vendor can read it, and which [sub-processors](/glossary/sub-processor) touch it. - How the vendor announces a model change, and whether you can stay on a fixed version. - How the vendor tells you about an incident, and who answers when you call. - Whether the system counts as high-risk under the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act), and which duties the contract leaves with you. - What happens to your data and prompts when the contract ends. ## Incident response plan When an AI system fails, its owner should not have to work out who to call. Write this call order down beside the register, with a name and a backup against each role. Inside the company, in this order: 1. The system owner named in the register, who limits or stops the system and keeps its logs and model version as they were. 2. The AI risk owner, who decides whether the incident is serious. 3. An executive who can approve a report and a message to customers. 4. Legal counsel, and whoever handles data breaches if personal data is involved. Outside the company, in this order: 5. The provider of the system, which is often the vendor. 6. The importer or distributor, if the system has one. 7. The market surveillance authority. 8. Affected customers, as your contracts require. For a high-risk system you deploy, Article 26 of the EU AI Act asks the deployer to give notice at once when it identifies a serious incident. The order is the provider first, then the importer or distributor and the market surveillance authority. Log the time each person learned of the incident. The page on [serious incident reporting](/glossary/serious-incident-reporting) says which moment starts the clock for a report and sets out the deadlines, so this plan does not repeat them.

rows.text: ## What this is Five axes, scored from zero to three, that give you a rough position before you pay anyone to check it properly. The axes match the ones in the [AI Readiness & Risk Assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment). This is the self-administered version, without the evidence behind it. ## The five axes | Axis | 0 — not started | 1 — informal | 2 — documented | 3 — evidenced | | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | | Strategy | No one has named which processes to automate first | Someone has an opinion, nothing written down | A ranked shortlist exists | The shortlist is reviewed by whoever owns the budget | | Data | No one knows what a vendor tool can see | A rough sense exists, not written down | A data classification table exists | The table is checked before a new tool is approved | | Delivery | Every pilot has stalled before production | One pilot is close to live | One system is live, unmonitored | A system is live, monitored, with a rollback path | | People | Only the original builder understands any AI system in use | One other person has read the code | A second person has changed it and shipped | Ownership is written down and handed over on a schedule | | Governance | No [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) exists | A register exists, out of date | A register exists, reviewed occasionally | The register is reviewed on a fixed schedule | ## Scoring it Score each axis from zero to three using the table above, then add the five scores for a total out of fifteen. A low total early on is common. It usually means nobody has written anything down yet, not that the engineering is behind. The five axes are not a substitute for the [NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) or [ISO/IEC 42001](https://www.iso.org/standard/42001). They are a rougher pass at the same territory, built to take an afternoon rather than an audit. ## What it is not It is not the Assessment, and it carries no evidence a reviewer would accept. A self-given three is a claim until someone outside your team checks what you have actually written down.

rows.text: ## What this is A worksheet for one recurring decision: build the workflow yourself, or buy a vendor's version of it. It will not choose for you. It gives the choice a written reason, which is what a board or a buyer asks for later. ## The six criteria | Criterion | Build tends to win when | Buy tends to win when | | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | Data residency | Customer data cannot leave your infrastructure by contract or by law | A vendor already holds a data-processing agreement you trust | | Customisation depth | The workflow is core to what makes your product different | The workflow looks like everyone else's version of the same task | | Time to a working version | You already have the engineers and the model access | Procurement moves faster than a hiring plan would | | Total cost over years | Usage is high enough that a per-call fee compounds | Usage is uncertain, and a fixed fee caps the downside | | Exit cost | You can rebuild the model calls without rebuilding the product | A second vendor could take over most of the same job | | Ownership when it breaks | An internal team already owns the surrounding process | A vendor's contract has a real answer to who to call | ## Scoring it Weight the six criteria for your situation, score build and buy against each one, and let the total argue with your gut feeling. A bought tool still needs an owner and a place in your [AI register](/glossary/ai-register). [NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) treats a vendor's model the same as one you trained. That sits under its MAP function (one of the framework's four functions). The risk to your customer does not care who wrote the code. ## Total cost of ownership The Total cost over years criterion needs a total cost of ownership (TCO) estimate, and a vendor quote covers only part of it. Fill in the categories in the table below, for build and for buy. Use the same horizon for both sides, long enough to cover the longest contract you would sign. For each side, add what you pay once to what you pay in every period of that horizon. | Side | Cost category | What to count | | ----- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Build | Engineering time | Engineer hours for the first version, and the work those engineers would otherwise ship | | Build | Maintenance | Upkeep as the model API, your libraries and your product change | | Build | Drift monitoring | The [evals](/glossary/evals) and review that catch quality slipping as models and data change | | Buy | Licence | The vendor's fee in the unit they meter it, and how it grows with your usage | | Buy | Integration | Connecting the tool to your data, login and workflows, plus the security review | | Buy | Lock-in | The cost of leaving: moving data out, redoing prompts and workflows, retraining staff | Take every amount from your own quotes and payroll, because this page lists no amounts. Use the same usage forecast on both sides, since the criteria table above shows that usage often decides which side costs less. Lock-in is the cost behind the Exit cost criterion, so fill in both together. ## What it is not It is not a procurement process, and it will not pick the vendor for you. It decides one thing: whether the job belongs inside your codebase or inside someone else's product. This is the call the [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) reviews every quarter, alongside the [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai) a team already bought without asking.

Most rows ask for a name, a place or a date; the rest ask for a decision. Only your company knows those. The owner and the test Fill this in first. This playbook asks for a written test so that the handover can end on a result, not only on a date. The [pilot article](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) says the new owner should have written at least one eval case and watched the rollback rehearsal. The [approach page](/approach) has a related test of whether your engineers can roll back a bad model without waiting on the outside lead. | Question | Your answer | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | | Who takes the role? Write one name. | | | Who decides whether to stop a launch, if that is a different person? | | | What must the new owner do without the outside lead before the role moves? | | | Who judges each check? | | | What counts as a pass? Write it so a third person could judge it. | | | What happens if the new owner is not ready on the planned date? | | ## Stage 2. What moves One row per item. Fill in who holds it today, who holds it after, where it lives and the date it moved. FCA handbook, an analogy. | | | | | | The list of AI systems | NIST asks for mechanisms to inventory AI systems. rows.text: ## What this is A policy file for whichever [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) you run, hosted or self-built. It is the config, not the gateway itself. The decisions live in a file your team reviews, not in a script only one engineer remembers. ## The policy schema | Key | What it controls | Example | | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | | allowed_models | Which providers and model versions a team may call | two named models, not an open list | | redact | Fields stripped before a prompt or response is logged or forwarded | email, national_id, card_number | | rate_limit | Calls per minute before the gateway queues or refuses | a ceiling per team, not per user | | log_retention | How long a request and response pair is kept | matches your data retention policy, not a default | | fallback | What happens if the primary provider is down | a named second provider, or a hard failure | ## Logging and retention The logging schema borrows its shape from [the EU AI Act's Article 12](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401689), which requires automatic event logs for high-risk systems. Not every call through a gateway is high-risk. The habit costs little to build in now. It is expensive to retrofit once a regulator or a customer asks first. The `allowed_models` and `log_retention` keys map to two [NIST SP 800-53](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final) control families: Access Control and Audit and Accountability. Procurement questionnaires often draw on this catalogue, even when nobody names it. ## What it is not It is not a gateway, and it will not stop a determined engineer from calling a model directly. It makes an unrouted call a [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai) finding. That is the layer the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) puts in front of a workflow before it counts as production.

rows.text: ## What this is Two weeks. I interview the people doing the work and read your systems and your vendor list. I write one memo you can hand to a board or a customer. ## What you keep You keep one document, whether or not you continue. It holds the readiness score, the gap list, and the three processes ranked by what automating them is worth this quarter. ## ISO/IEC 42001 gap assessment The gap list compares your company with [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001), the standard for an AI management system that an accredited body can certify. It shows where you fall short of what the standard asks. This is a gap assessment, not a certification. An accredited body runs the independent audit that grants certification, and the [certification FAQ](/faq/can-you-get-us-iso-iec-42001-certified-or-just-a-working-system) covers the difference between a working system and a certificate. ## Why it is two weeks and not two days A readiness claim you cannot show evidence for is worth nothing in a security review. I read the code, talk to the people who use the tools, and check what your vendors actually do with your data. Two weeks is the shortest span in which I can do all three.

rows.text: Governance has a bad name in small companies because most of what is sold under that name is written for a bank. A three hundred person company does not need a committee, a maturity model or a consultant to run a workshop. It needs four things that fit on a shared drive and get updated when something changes.

rows.text: The fourth is a named owner: one person whose job description says they own AI risk and who has the authority to stop a launch. rows.text: A security review of an AI system usually starts with one question: what is actually running. If the honest answer takes a week of digging through chat logs and old tickets, the review stalls before it reaches architecture or data flows. An AI system register is the fix: one document listing every AI system a company runs, who owns it, and how risky it is.
